fatal_errors: The hypothesis treats ethanol oxidation as the target reaction, whereas the target catalyst was investigated mechanistically for acidic HER and alkaline HOR.
It does not reconstruct the Pd nanocube core with an approximately five-layer, randomly mixed PtRuFeCoNi {100} shell, instead inventing a generic Pt-rich, high-index or stepped surface.

The proposed d-band/CO-poisoning mechanism omits the target's near-thermoneutral hydrogen adsorption, Fe-to-Ru electron transfer and Ru HER sites, potential-dependent Pt/Co/Ni hydroxyl chemistry during HOR, and kinetic stabilization of the metastable shell.
The cited ethanol-oxidation evidence concerns different multielement catalysts and does not establish the claimed Pt-rich surface, high-index facets, or electronic mechanism for the target material.

Changing or removing secondary metals alters site ensembles and composition as well as electronic coupling, so the proposed comparison cannot uniquely attribute any performance change to d-band modulation.
explanation: The response is testable at a generic level, and its matched-morphology composition comparison plus electrochemical measurements could probe whether secondary metals matter. However, it reconstructs neither the target material nor its reactions, conditions, controls, structural evolution, element-specific active sites, or quantitative outcomes. The only overlap is the broad idea that multielement electronic interactions tune adsorption. Evidence E1 even cautions that a single d-band-center description may be inadequate for heterogeneous HEA surfaces, while E2 concerns HOR on a different nanowire catalyst and E3 supports EOR performance of a different ordered octonary material without validating the proposed high-index-facet mechanism. Direct spectroscopy or adsorption-energy measurements would also be needed to distinguish electronic modulation from ensemble and structural effects.
